claims.text: Controlled thermomechanical processing that minimizes grain-boundary solute segregation will retain toughness in CoCrFeNiAl0.3.
Minimizing grain-boundary solute segregation prevents the formation of brittle intergranular precipitates.
Excessive grain-boundary segregation promotes brittle intergranular phases in CoCrFeNiAl0.3.
Systematic cold deformation followed by annealing at 800°C for 1–4 hours and controlled cooling can produce variants with minimized or enhanced boundary segregation.
Intergranular precipitates form as a result of solute segregation.
Optimized processing reduces solute accumulation at grain boundaries.
Reduced solute accumulation at grain boundaries limits brittle intergranular precipitate formation.
Brittle intergranular phases act as crack-initiation sites.
Crack initiation at brittle intergranular phases lowers toughness.
Samples processed to minimize grain-boundary segregation will have higher fracture toughness than the uncontrolled-processing baseline.
Samples processed to minimize grain-boundary segregation will exhibit delayed crack propagation relative to the baseline.
Samples with greater grain-boundary segregation will exhibit a rapid decrease in toughness.
Conventional processing that does not control boundary segregation produces random segregation levels and corresponding variation in mechanical properties.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply to CoCrFeNiAl0.3 within the stated cold-deformation and annealing conditions.
Composition changes or processing outside the proposed bounds may activate additional toughness-controlling mechanisms.
Other microstructural effects may overlap with the effects of grain-boundary segregation on toughness.
